text: I’ll model the full 360° annular fluid domain in metres. I’ll use piecewise half-cosine axial blends between the three specified stations; this exactly meets each radius and gives zero slope at the inlet, midpoint, and outlet (a C1-smooth profile). The initial mesh will be a coarse unstructured volume mesh, with the four CAD faces tagged before export. First I’m checking the installed build123d API needed to construct the revolved fluid solid directly.

The available API supports direct spline edges and revolution. I’ll now construct the meridional annulus from named profile edges, revolve it about the x-axis, and inspect the resulting topology and dimensions before exporting anything. The sampled cosine profiles preserve the requested station radii exactly; I’ll quantify spline interpolation error separately.

The revolved result is a valid single solid with exactly four boundary faces and the intended 0–0.9 m extent. I’ll generate a coarse visual preview and plot axial cuts of both profiles, while measuring the three requested radii directly from the spline curves. Face patch association will remain tied to the named generating edges rather than bounding-box position.

The preview confirms the intended converging annulus and the core-cowl mid-duct bulge. All six requested radii measure exactly at 0, 0.45, and 0.9 m. Next I’ll test the direct edge-revolution operation so each boundary face can inherit the name of its generating profile edge without positional heuristics.

Edges do not expose a method-form revolution in this installed build123d release. I’ll use the module-level revolution operator on each named edge and compare the generated faces to the solid boundary by OpenCASCADE identity; this keeps patch assignment topological rather than coordinate-based.

Module-level revolution does not return a surface for a bare edge, so I’ll associate each solid face with its named generating edge by the exact swept-area invariant (surface of revolution area, or annular end area). The four expected areas are distinct, making the mapping unique and independent of face order or bounding boxes. I’ll then export all four patches together so shared triangulation seams weld correctly.
The area calculation hit NumPy 2’s removal of `trapz`; no files were exported. I’ll replace it with `trapezoid` and inspect the exporter signature before making the corrected export call.
I’ll re-emit the corrected export cell with its own exporter import so the final replayable script has no dependency on the failed cell.

The mapping was unique and correct, but the guard tolerance was 2.0×10⁻⁶ m² while the sampled-spline versus analytic-cosine area difference reached 2.47×10⁻⁶ m². I’ll use a 5×10⁻⁶ m² guard; this is still orders of magnitude below separation between candidate face areas.

The four STLs are now exported from one tessellation; their welded union has 13,500 triangles, zero open edges, zero winding conflicts, and zero non-manifold edges. I’ll create a coarse Cartesian background mesh (about 0.03 m cells) extending beyond both axial caps, then use `snappyHexMesh` with a point inside the bypass annulus to retain only the fluid region and preserve the four named surface patches.
The meshing dictionaries are in place. I’ll build and check the coarse background mesh first, before surface cutting.
The coarse background mesh has 34,816 uniform 30 mm cells and fully covers the cowl. I’ll now cut and snap it to the watertight four-patch surface.

`snappyHexMesh` stopped before modifying the background mesh because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes`/`fvSolution` dictionaries even for meshing. I’ll add minimal meshing-only dictionaries, without solver fields or boundary conditions.
The required meshing dictionaries now exist. I’ll rerun surface cutting and snapping.

OpenFOAM 2512 also requires an explicit empty `features` list when feature files are not used. I’ll add that required entry; the geometry was read successfully and no mesh changes occurred before the stop.
I’ll rerun `snappyHexMesh` with the completed 2512 dictionary.

The coarse snapped mesh completed with 52,834 cells and no quality errors under the mesher’s configured limits. I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect patch counts and geometric bounds.

`checkMesh` passes: one connected region, four correctly named patches, 52,834 cells, maximum non-orthogonality 40.5°, maximum skewness 1.07, and mesh volume 0.288203 m³ versus CAD volume 0.288558 m³ (0.12% lower from surface discretization). I’ll render a cutaway of the actual volume mesh to visually check annular connectivity and surface conformity.
The mesh itself is valid; only the visualization utility rejected an outdated `-noFields` spelling. I’ll inspect this installed utility’s options before rendering.
The installed option is `-no-fields`. I’ll now render the cutaway from the exported volume mesh.

The cutaway shows a single continuous annular volume, with the inner core excluded and both axial annular faces resolved. I’ll make one final quantitative smoothness check on the actual spline geometry by finite-differencing its radius near each join; the half-cosine design target is zero slope at all three stations.

The actual spline is continuous and smooth through the midpoint. Finite-difference slopes are small (largest magnitude 0.00264, about 0.15°); exact zero slope was a blending assumption rather than a user requirement, and spline interpolation introduces this small deviation while retaining exact station radii. I’ll now submit the completed mesh to the final checks with no expected advisory waivers.

The final gate confirms full coverage—every one of the 13,500 surface triangles belongs to exactly one of the four requested patches—but reports that fact as an advisory requiring acknowledgement. I’ll waive `coverage` because this exact one-patch-per-face partition is correct for the closed bypass-fluid boundary.
